query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local short-range chemical ordering at Al- and Ni-rich sites governs the stable fcc/B2 dual-phase microstructure in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, enabling simultaneous enhancement of high-temperature strength, corrosion/radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness by coherently pinning phase boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a baseline dual-phase (fcc + B2) microstructure prepared under standard solutionizing and quenching conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary short-range order through controlled heat treatments (different temperatures/times) and targeted compositional adjustments (e.g., small additions of Al or Ni) while maintaining overall alloy stoichiometry.
generation.conditions: Characterize and test mechanical behavior, corrosion/radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness from −196 °C to 900 °C under identical metallurgical and environmental exposures.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of local short-range order that influences nucleation and spatial distribution of B2 domains within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced short-range ordering at Al- and Ni-rich lattice sites stabilizes the B2 domains, strengthening the alloy and preventing intergranular deterioration under radiation, oxidation, or low-temperature embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stronger and more chemically stable B2–fcc interface with higher hardness, improved corrosion/radiation resistance, and superior cryogenic ductility as short-range order is strengthened, relative to a baseline alloy with reduced local ordering.
generation.baseline: Samples from the same composition subjected to minimal ordering treatments, expected to show stronger single-phase tendencies and inferior multi-property synergy.
generation.boundary: At extreme Al content or at temperatures beyond the critical ordering range, the stabilizing effect from short-range ordering may fade, causing phase coarsening and reduced property benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While short-range order is hypothesized to be the dominant factor, secondary effects (e.g., interfacial segregation, grain-boundary chemistry) cannot be fully excluded without further data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple alloy batches with identical nominal compositions but use different heat treatment protocols to induce systematically varied levels of short-range order. Then measure phase stability and mechanical/environmental properties from cryogenic to high-temperature regimes.
measurements: Atom probe tomography to quantify local chemical ordering
In situ X-ray diffraction to track phase evolution
Nanoindentation or hardness testing to assess mechanical strength
Corrosion and radiation damage testing to gauge environmental resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significantly altering short-range order does not consistently change the fraction, morphology, or stability of the B2 and fcc phases, nor measurably affect mechanical or environmental properties, then the hypothesized role of local short-range ordering in governing the dual-phase stability and performance is refuted.

The senary and the quinaries are compared using experimental techniques including X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, X‐ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and first principles hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations. Chemical short‐range order and bond length distances have been determined both at the experimental and computational level. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: Early studies on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni focused on designing eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with dual-phase (fcc + B2) microstructures for improved castability and high fracture strength (2014). Subsequent efforts showed that ultrafine-grained, hierarchically heterogeneous lamellae in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (2019) could further enhance the strength–ductility balance. However, despite these advances, it remains unclear which fundamental factor most directly stabilizes the multi-phase microstructure across a wide temperature range, enabling the simultaneous improvement of high-temperature mechanical strength, environmental and radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
decision.unsolved: It is still unresolved how to rationalize the role of local chemical and structural order in dictating the stability of the fcc/B2 dual-phase microstructure. Various observations suggest that partial ordering or clustering along Al- and Ni-rich sites could contribute to stable co-existence of ductile and hard phases, but direct experimental evidence linking this local ordering to phase stability (and to performance in high-temperature, cryogenic, and radiation conditions) is still missing. A single mechanistic framework explaining how these local short-range ordering and lattice distortions jointly govern phase evolution—thus retaining desirable high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness—has yet to be conclusively validated. A key question is whether it is indeed local chemical ordering that pins and stabilizes the B2-fcc interfaces under diverse conditions, or whether other mechanisms (e.g., entropic effects alone, or second-phase precipitation not driven by short-range order) dominate in controlling phase stability.
decision.lever: Systematically tune and quantify local short-range order in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni via heat treatments (varying temperature/time) combined with in-situ diffraction, atom probe tomography, and first-principles or CALPHAD-based simulations. Use a baseline alloy with a known dual-phase state, then compare to samples processed to reduce or enhance short-range chemical ordering, testing mechanical properties, radiation tolerance, and corrosion resistance across cryogenic to high temperatures. If stable fcc/B2 boundaries and property synergies correlate directly with short-range order signatures, the hypothesis is validated. If significant changes in local ordering do not alter phase stability and properties, it will falsify this mechanism. This approach leverages prior evidence of eutectic fcc/B2 microstructure formation in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni EHEAs and targets the core question of how local ordering controls phase evolution and multi-property performance.
decision.why: This step isolates the effect of local short-range order on B2–fcc stability by comparing systematically heat-treated samples with distinct ordering levels, directly testing the proposed mechanistic link between local chemical order, stable multi-phase microstructures, and the synergy of high-temperature performance, corrosion/radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness observed in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni EHEAs.
